newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt jumps higher celebrating U.S. gains.
newsitem.headline: German debt jumps higher celebrating U.S. gains.

text.p: German debt raced higher in early Wednesday trading, attempting to keep pace with U.S. market gains amassed on Tuesday after the central bank predicted inflation would remain under control for some time.

By 0808 GMT the German September Bund futures contract traded on Frankfurt's DTB exchange stood at 103.37, up 36 basis points and the benchmark 10-year cash bond was trading at 103.76, compared with a 103.43 close on Tuesday.
"We are simply following the U.S. market, there is nothing else driving us here," one dealer said, explained the morning's unexpectedly vigorous rise in prices.
Delighted by a sharp jump in U.S. Treasury prices on Tuesday, German bund futures jumped to open trade on Wednesday at 103.50 after having ended the session at 103.01 on Tuesday.

U.S. Treasury prices climbed after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress that the economy's growth was slowing for now and that inflation this year would be quite modest, jettisoning fears of an imminent rate hike in the U.S.

But dealers also said the morning's gains could not be fully maintained. "We raced higher as domestic investors bought but there was some selling on the international side, so there was a bit of profit-taking all the same," a dealer said.
Dealers said while the general direction for German debt remained pointed higher, there could be more profit-taking throughout the session.
"The rise was just a bit sudden and we might have to go lower before moving higher," another dealer said.
Looking ahead dealers said the market's next goal might be the 103.75 level and after that 104.04 could become a tempting target. Support could be seen at the 103.15 level dealers said.
The session's activities will be further guided by U.S. market movements, dealers said, noting little attention was being paid to anything else.
"German numbers are really of very little interest at the moment, no one is paying much attention," said a dealer, commenting on several German state inflation numbers.
Hesse, Bavaria and North Rhine-Westphalia released inflation data showing a slight blip higher, reflecting the impact of the depreciating German currency, economists said.

"Slowly the effects of the weaker mark are having an impact on inflation levels," said Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt, predicting German inflation levels are likely to blip a bit higher in coming months. But he also predicted the Bundesbank would take no action now.
Holger Fahrinkrug, senior Germany economist at UBS in Frankfurt, agreed that the Bundesbank has no reason to adjust interest rates at this time even as the dollar is moving higher.

"There is absolutely no reason to panic," Fahrinkrug assured after the German inflation numbers came out, noting that the increase was caused by one-off price hikes and that the the central bank would not risk trampling Germany's fragile economic recovery with a rate hike now.
The Bundesbank will meet on Thursday.
